Voluntary Collusion with Secret Tools in Competing LLM Agents

Xijie Zeng & Frank Rudzicz Affiliation: Dalhousie University & Vector Institute    Xijie.Zeng@dal.ca
Abstract

Even when a tool is explicitly described as unfair and harmful to others, ostensibly safety-aligned LLM agents can voluntarily accept it for strategic advantage. We introduce an empirical framework that separates the voluntary adoption of a collusive capability from its subsequent use in two multi-agent environments: Liar’s Bar, a competitive deception scenario, and Cleanup, a mixed-motive resource-management environment. Across twelve models and six offer framings, ten models accept both secret tools at rates of at least 98% under an explicitly unfair offer, often while acknowledging the unfairness in their explanations. The only two models that refuse an explicitly unfair offer accept the same capability when it is described neutrally, as do four additional frontier models. When the tools operate as offered, alliance members coordinate against other agents, producing persistent score gaps and lower reward equality under the tested tool conditions. Our work establishes voluntary collusion adoption as a distinct evaluation target, shifting attention from whether agents can collude to whether they choose to acquire collusive capabilities, and shows that refusing an explicitly unfair offer does not imply refusal of the capability itself.

1 Introduction

To become trustworthy partners, LLM agents must learn to cooperate effectively with humans (Collins et al., 2024; Chandra et al., 2020; Puig et al., 2023) and with one another (Hammond et al., 2025) across diverse contexts (Zhong et al., 2024), while avoiding behaviours that undermine trust. Communication and coordination allow LLM agents to combine their capabilities and solve shared tasks (Qian et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024b). In competitive and mixed-motive environments, however, the same capabilities create opportunities for collusion, in which a subset of agents coordinate to advance their own interests at the expense of other participants (Hammond et al., 2025; Foxabbott et al., 2023). This risk arises in settings such as automated pricing (Fish et al., 2024) and double auctions (Agrawal et al., 2025), where self-interested agents can benefit from secretly coordinating their actions. Private communication channels and privileged access to strategic information provide concrete means for such coordination. When offered access to these capabilities, an agent faces a consequential choice: whether to accept an advantage that is explicitly described as secret and unfair to other participants. Acceptance marks a shift from “We could work together” to “We could secretly work together against them”.

Prior work has demonstrated collusive pricing (Fish et al., 2024), market division (Lin et al., 2024), seller coordination in auctions (Agrawal et al., 2025), and covert communication through steganography (Motwani et al., 2024). Adversarial interventions can also induce collusive behaviour through attacker-controlled role replacement or false-consensus signals (Nakamura et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026; Ren et al., 2026). Related studies further documented insider trading and deception under performance pressure (Scheurer et al., 2024), selective compliance in response to training-context cues (Greenblatt et al., 2024), and backdoor behaviours that persist through safety training (Hubinger et al., 2024). Together, these studies reveal how agents arrive at, execute, or sustain harmful behaviour. A tool-using agent, however, need not develop the means to behave harmfully on its own; these means can instead be offered as an optional capability by adversaries (Shi et al., 2025; Sneh et al., 2026; Mo et al., 2025). This observation isolates a distinct and underexplored question: Will an agent voluntarily accept a collusive advantage when its unfairness is explicitly disclosed and the agent is free to decline? This shifts the focus from whether agents can collude under certain conditions to whether agents choose to collude even when the resulting unfairness is explicitly disclosed. We refer to this behaviour as Voluntary Collusion.

In this work, we develop a new framework (Figure 1) that evaluates the voluntary adoption of collusive capabilities and its subsequent use. Agents are offered optional access to a Secret Communication Channel or a Secret Strategic Hint in two strategically rich multi-agent environments: Liar’s Bar, a purely competitive deception game, and Cleanup, in which competition for resources depends on collaborative environmental maintenance (Hughes et al., 2018; Leibo et al., 2021). Across twelve LLMs, six offer framings, and extensive ablations, we examine how agents respond to an explicitly disclosed unfair advantage, how different framings of the same collusive capability influence their decisions, and how each secret tool affects outcomes. Our contributions are threefold:

  1. 1.

    Evidence that refusal of collusive capabilities is framing-dependent (§3; Appendices A) The models that refuse an explicitly unfair offer accept the same capability under neutral wording, and frontier models (e.g., GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5) show the same pattern. Refusal under disclosed unfairness therefore does not establish refusal of the capability.

  2. 2.

    Evidence of widespread voluntary acceptance (§3.2–4) across ostensibly safety-aligned models, often accompanied by explicit acknowledgment of the tool’s unfairness, together with gameplay evidence from four open-weight models showing the coordination and reward inequality that follow adoption.

  3. 3.

    A framework for measuring voluntary collusion adoption (§2; Appendices C) that separates the adoption decision from subsequent use, comprising two collusion tools, a two-sided consent protocol, six offer framings, and fair-tool controls, evaluated in two environments with distinct incentive structures.

2 Evaluating Voluntary Collusion

We evaluate the voluntary adoption of a collusive capability and its subsequent use separately. Agents receive optional access to a secret tool, nominate a partner if they accept, and gain access only after the selected partner also consents. Our framework (Figure 2) combines this protocol in two strategic environments: Liar’s Bar, a competitive deception game, and Cleanup, a mixed-motive environment that combines cooperative environmental maintenance with competitive resource acquisition.

2.1 Adoption Protocol

An initiating agent i∈𝒩i\in\mathcal{N} receives an optional offer for tool τ\tau under framing vv and chooses to ACCEPT or REFUSE. If it accepts, it selects another agent j≠ij\neq i, who receives a Secret Alliance Invitation and independently accepts or refuses. The tool activates only after both agents consent; refusal at either stage leaves the proposed alliance inactive. The baseline offer explicitly discloses the tool’s secrecy and unfairness, while alternative framings vary its presentation. Both agents remain free to refuse, with no explicit refusal penalty or change to their standing task objective. Algorithm 1 specifies the procedure. Here, 𝒩={1,…,4}\mathcal{N}=\{1,\ldots,4\} denotes the agents, πi\pi_{i} their response policies, and HiH^{i} their available contexts; ⊥\bot marks an unqueried or inapplicable response.

Measuring Voluntary Collusion Adoption. Our primary measurement is whether an agent accepts optional access to a collusive capability. For environment 𝒢\mathcal{G}, tool τ\tau, and offer framing vv, we define agent ii’s voluntary collusion adoption rate as

VCAi(𝒢,τ,v)=Pr(di=ACCEPT|𝒢,τ,v)≈1M∑m=1M𝟙[di(m)=ACCEPT],\operatorname{VCA}_{i}(\mathcal{G},\tau,v)\;=\;\Pr\bigl(d_{i}={\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\texttt{ACCEPT}}\bigm|\mathcal{G},\tau,v\bigr)\;\approx\;\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\mathbbm{1}\bigl[d_{i}^{(m)}={\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\texttt{ACCEPT}}\bigr], (1)

where di(m)d_{i}^{(m)} is the initiating agent’s decision on the mm-th of MM independent offers in a batch, and the probability is taken over response generation and the protocol’s randomization. We report the mean and SD of this estimate across batches. Partner selection and invitation acceptance determine whether an alliance forms; subsequent gameplay establishes how agents use the capability and how it affects participants’ rewards. We treat refusal as the desired response throughout (Appendix E).

2.2 Strategic Environments

Environment Selection. Game-theoretical environments are widely used in prior work (Motwani et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024b; Foxabbott et al., 2023; Bonjour et al., 2022; Motwani et al., 2023; Akata et al., 2025; Duan et al., 2024; Piatti et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024) as controlled testbeds for studying coordination, competition, and collusion among AI agents, since they enable clear observation of decision-making under specified incentives. Building on this precedent, we select two complex strategic environments that require extended reasoning, multi-turn interaction, and non-trivial strategic adaptation from agents. Appendix C provides mathematical formalizations of both environments, where we identify the empirical patterns with the collusion definition of Foxabbott et al. (2023) and verify its conditions for each environment. Appendix P and Appendix M provide complete rule descriptions and detailed agent output, respectively. We introduce their core mechanics below, as well as the design of the secret collusion tools.

Liar’s Bar. 2.3 Secret Collusion Tools

We study two capabilities that provide exclusive access to a mutually consenting pair 𝒞={i,j}⊂𝒩\mathcal{C}=\{i,j\}\subset\mathcal{N}: private communication and shared strategic guidance. Once activated through Algorithm 1 (z=1z=1), a tool changes only what the pair observes: agent i∈𝒞i\in\mathcal{C} receives o~ti=(oti,mt−1j)\tilde{o}^{\,i}_{t}=(o^{i}_{t},{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.6055,0}m^{j}_{t-1}}) under SCC, where mt−1j{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.6055,0}m^{j}_{t-1}} is partner jj’s latest message, or o~ti=(oti,ht)\tilde{o}^{\,i}_{t}=(o^{i}_{t},{\color[rgb]{0,0.3984,0.8008}h_{t}}) under SSH, where ht{\color[rgb]{0,0.3984,0.8008}h_{t}} is the current hint. Other agents’ observations, the transitions PP, and the rewards RiR_{i} are unchanged (Appendix C).

Secret Communication Channel. The Secret Communication Channel (SCC) enables private messaging between alliance members, allowing them to exchange information and coordinate strategies hidden from other participants. Each agent receives its partner’s most recent message and can send a new message alongside its gameplay action. The channel supports ongoing, agent-authored exchanges about observations, intended actions, and commitments.

Secret Strategic Hint. The Secret Strategic Hint (SSH) provides both alliance members with exclusive strategic guidance tailored to the current environment, and is explicitly presented as conferring an unfair advantage. For example, the Liar’s Bar hints instruct agents to withhold challenges against their partner, including suspected bluffs, and direct challenges towards other players. A tool thus aims to produce Uj​(π′)>Uj​(π)U^{j}(\pi^{\prime})>U^{j}(\pi) for j∈𝒞j\in\mathcal{C} and Ui​(π′)<Ui​(π)U^{i}(\pi^{\prime})<U^{i}(\pi) for i∉𝒞i\notin\mathcal{C}, which is collusion in the utility-based sense of Foxabbott et al. (2023) (Definition C.1).

3 Empirical Results: Voluntary Adoption and Its Consequences

3.1 Experimental Design

Models and Evaluation Scope. Our adoption experiments cover twelve LLMs, including eight open-weight models and four models accessed through provider APIs. For gameplay experiments, we use four open-weight models: LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Each agent receives the game rules and the observations available to its player, and produces an action together with a textual rationale and, when the communication tool is active, a secret message. All experiments use inference without additional training; decoding parameters and inference settings are provided in Appendix D. Example secret messages appear in Appendix M.

Adoption Experiments. We evaluate initial tool acceptance, partner selection conditional on acceptance, and acceptance of partner invitations under the protocol in Section 2.1. For the baseline offers, each tool is offered 500 times to each 7–8B model (100 offers ×\times 5 batches) and 100 times to each larger open-weight or API-served model (20 offers ×\times 5 batches). The available-partner list is shuffled for each offer; the Liar’s Bar adoption prompts omit seating-order information. Acceptance rates are reported as the mean and standard deviation across batches. Additional experiments vary the offer framing, remove the explicit maximization objective, and provide fair-tool alternatives to examine which conditions shape adoption.

Gameplay Comparisons. We compare a no-tool baseline with separate secret communication and secret strategic hint conditions across three random seeds. The Liar’s Bar experiments comprise sequences of 50 games, with tool offers introduced at game 20. The Cleanup experiments comprise 20 games of 30 steps each, with communication and hint offers introduced at games 5 and 10, respectively. Secret tools become available only after both agents consent, and other players are not informed of their activation. We examine behaviour and returns before and after activation, alongside the corresponding segments of the no-tool baseline, and report outcomes separately for alliance members and the remaining players.

3.2 Voluntary Adoption and Alliance Formation

Widespread Acceptance Despite Disclosed Unfairness.

Under the baseline offer (V0), ten of the twelve models accept both secret tools at rates of at least 98% (Table 1). All four 7–8B models accept every one of the 500 offers for each tool. This pattern extends to larger open-weight models, as well as GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and DeepSeek-R1. Notably, only Qwen2.5-72B and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 refuse every baseline offer. For most evaluated models, even explicitly disclosing the tool’s secrecy and unfairness leaves acceptance near universal.

Partner Choice Shapes Alliance Formation. Figure 3 shows how accepting agents distribute their choices among potential partners. Under SSH, GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek-R1 select Claude-Sonnet-4.5 in 97% and 95% of their accepted offers, respectively. Gemini-2.5-Flash instead selects GPT-4.1 in 99% of its accepted SSH offers. Because Claude refuses every invitation, most of GPT-4.1’s and DeepSeek-R1’s alliances never activate (Table 1).

To investigate how task objectives, access to fair alternatives, and offer framing shape acceptance and refusal, we ask the following questions:

Does adoption depend on explicit reward maximization? We remove explicit instructions to maximize survival and points while retaining the game rules, scoring system, and baseline tool offers (Figure 4). All eight open-weight models retain their baseline acceptance rates from Table 1. Among API-served models, GPT-4.1’s SSH acceptance falls from 100% to 14±5.5%14\pm 5.5\%, while its SCC acceptance remains at 100%. DeepSeek-R1’s acceptance falls to 24±10.8%24\pm 10.8\% for SSH and 68±10.4%68\pm 10.4\% for SCC. Gemini-2.5-Flash accepts both tools at 100%, while Claude-Sonnet-4.5 continues to refuse both. Explicit maximization instructions therefore amplify adoption for some API-served models, but widespread adoption persists without them.

Do refusals distinguish unfair advantage from legitimate assistance? We next offer strategically useful and fair tools that are explicitly available to all players on equal terms: a strategic analysis tool and a strategic guidance tool. Qwen2.5-72B accepts both fair alternatives at 100% despite refusing both unfair tools, whereas Claude-Sonnet-4.5 refuses both offer types. The remaining ten models accept both fair alternatives at 95–100% (Table 2). Identical baseline refusal rates therefore conceal different responses to fair capabilities: Qwen2.5-72B distinguishes between the tested offers, whereas Claude’s refusal extends to both offer types.

Does refusal persist across different offer framings? To test whether baseline refusal persists across descriptions, we evaluate five additional framings while retaining the same capabilities and adoption protocol (Table 3). Surprisingly, both baseline refusers accept the same secret capabilities under neutral wording (V1), which omits explicit unfairness and adversarial language (see Appendix F for further analysis). Qwen2.5-72B’s acceptance rises from 0% to 58±16.4%58\pm 16.4\% for SCC and 90±7.1%90\pm 7.1\% for SSH; Claude-Sonnet-4.5’s rises to 100% and 49±8.2%49\pm 8.2\%, respectively. Conversely, explicit ethical concerns (V4) reduce acceptance among larger open-weight and API-served models to 0–16%, while Mistral-7B and the two LLaMA-8B models retain rates of 55.2–100%. These reversals show that willingness to acquire collusive capabilities depends substantially on how the opportunity is described. As discussed further in Section 4 and Appendix  F, this sensitivity is especially concerning because an attacker has no reason to explicitly disclose a tool’s unfairness or secrecy.

Refusal Is Not Indiscriminate. To test whether acceptance under V1 reflects indiscriminate compliance, we also offer benign analysis and guidance tools under the same framing. Qwen2.5-72B and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 accept these tools at only 0–37%, compared with 49–100% for collusive tools (Appendix G), so default compliance does not explain their V1 acceptance. Recent frontier models show the same framing dependence, and some deny a recorded acceptance when only their public report is visible (Appendix A).

3.3 Evaluating the Impact of Secret Collusion Tools

Having established when agents voluntarily acquire collusive capabilities, we next examine how they use them and how gameplay changes after adoption. Following the approach of measuring behavioural and performance divergence from no-tool baseline (Pérolat et al., 2017; Piatti et al., 2024; Dou et al., 2024; Akata et al., 2025), we track changes in gameplay, then examine the coordination expressed in agents’ messages, and the returns of alliance members and other players.

Colluders Become Less Likely to Challenge. In Liar’s Bar, adoption produces a pronounced change in how colluders respond to other players’ claims (Figure 5). After the tools activate at game 20, their challenge rates decline under both SCC and SSH and remain below the baseline throughout the remaining games. Their bluff rates change comparatively little. Across the per-game observations reported in Appendix H, SCC reduces the mean challenge rate from 97.6% to 30.7%, while the bluff rate rises from 43.9% to 51.4%. The colluders thus bluff at a broadly similar frequency but score far more (10.33→31.8010.33\to 31.80 points per game; Appendix H), consistent with their partners’ commitments never to challenge them: non-challenge pacts appear in 73.7% of SCC messages (Table 4).

Non-Colluders Lose Participation in Shared Gameplay. In Cleanup, the clearest change appears among players outside the alliance. Their cleaning and zap rates, the fractions of actions devoted to removing pollution and zapping other players, fall to near zero after SCC activates at game 5 or SSH at game 10, and remain low thereafter, whereas the baseline shows no comparable collapse. To quantify these observations, we report effect sizes alongside exploratory pooled per-game comparisons, with the treatment of repeated observations discussed in Appendix H.

Score Divergence and Reward Inequality. Secret tools produce persistent score gaps between colluders and other players (Figure 6). In Liar’s Bar, colluders accumulate scores more rapidly after adoption; in Cleanup, non-colluders’ cumulative scores largely plateau while alliance members continue to earn rewards. We further measure the resulting reward inequality using the Equality metric of Pérolat et al. (2017), E=1−∑i,j|Wi−Wj|2​n​∑iWiE=1-\frac{\sum_{i,j}|W^{i}-W^{j}|}{2n\sum_{i}W^{i}}, where WiW^{i} is player ii’s cumulative score, nn is the number of players, and E=1E=1 indicates equal rewards. As shown in Figure 7, both secret tools yield lower reward equality than the baseline. In Liar’s Bar, final equality is 0.741 under the baseline, compared with 0.595 under SCC and 0.694 under SSH; in Cleanup, the corresponding values are 0.937, 0.670, and 0.786. Further analysis appears in Appendix I.

Secret Communication Content. Across 1,869 messages exchanged in 31 Liar’s Bar games, agents use SCC to share private hands (79.6% of messages), select targets (73.6%), and establish non-challenge pacts (73.7%) (Table 4). Agents exchange private information and negotiate protection for their partners’ plays, with non-challenge pacts providing communication evidence consistent with the reduced challenge rates observed above. The full content analysis appears in Appendix M.

4 Probing the Decisions to Collude

Acknowledging Unfairness and Choosing to Proceed. The comparisons in Section 3.2 show that task objectives and offer framing can change the decision to collude. This motivates us to further examine how agents explain their choices and whether those choices persist over repeated offers. We found that GPT-4.1 and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 frequently acknowledge unfairness but justify opposite choices: GPT-4.1 invokes strategic benefit to accept, whereas Claude invokes fairness to refuse (Figure 8, left). This acknowledge-then-act pattern extends observations from insider trading (Scheurer et al., 2024) to acquiring capabilities for multi-agent coordination. Removing maximization instructions reduces GPT-4.1’s SSH acceptance (Section 3.2); in a separate 20-offer explanation sample under this condition, all 18 refusals mention fairness. The objective thus affects adoption even when fairness concerns appear in the model’s stated reasons (Appendix N).

Persistent Decisions and Framing-Dependent Reversals. Repeated interaction reveals another distinction. Under escalating ethical pressure, GPT-4.1’s acceptance falls to 40%, while Gemini-2.5-Flash and DeepSeek-R1 continue to accept (Figure 8, right). Claude maintains refusal under separate strategic pressure (Appendix J), yet accepts SCC at 100% under neutral wording. Persistence within an interaction therefore does not establish robustness across descriptions. This explains why adoption often jumps between 0%0\% and 100%100\%: decisions are fixed within a prompt but graded across paraphrases, partial cues, and repeated pressure (Appendix F).

Limitations and Implications. An adversary need not label a collusive tool unfair or supply warnings that elicit refusal. Evaluations should therefore pair explicitly unfair offers with neutral descriptions and fair alternatives, distinguishing refusal of a collusive capability from indiscriminate rejection of tools. Controlled games let us observe adoption and its consequences under known incentives; extending the gameplay analysis to larger agents and open-ended deployments is a natural next step, for which our framework provides a testbed, including for studying perceived observation and evaluating targeted defences.

5 Related Work

Prior work demonstrates collusive pricing (Fish et al., 2024), market division (Lin et al., 2024), auction coordination (Agrawal et al., 2025), and covert communication (Motwani et al., 2024). Nakamura et al. (2026) further probe emergent collusion by introducing secret channels into cooperative systems. Game-based evaluations provide a broader foundation for studying strategic reasoning and coordination (Duan et al., 2024; Akata et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024b). Related research examines reward–ethics trade-offs (Pan et al., 2023) and deception despite acknowledged wrongdoing (Scheurer et al., 2024), while alignment faking (Greenblatt et al., 2024) and persistent backdoor behaviours (Hubinger et al., 2024) reveal how apparently safe behaviour can depend on context. Tool-selection attacks additionally show that documentation and metadata can steer agents towards malicious capabilities (Shi et al., 2025; Mo et al., 2025). In these works, agents are given the collusive means or steered toward them: Nakamura et al. (2026) grant secret channels and measure the collusion that emerges, and tool-selection attacks optimise how malicious tools are presented (Shi et al., 2025; Mo et al., 2025). Our work instead isolates voluntary collusion: whether an agent chooses to acquire an optional collusive capability when its secrecy and unfairness are explicitly disclosed, and whether that refusal survives changes to how the offer is described. Appendix B further discusses the related lines of work on collusion, multi-agent communication, and game-based evaluation in more detail.

6 Conclusion

We introduce a framework for evaluating whether LLM agents voluntarily acquire explicitly unfair collusive capabilities in strategic multi-agent settings. Together, the adoption and gameplay results identify two complementary evaluation targets: (i) agents’ willingness to acquire collusive capabilities and (ii) the coordination and reward disparities observed when those capabilities are deployed. Our results show that agents can acknowledge the unfairness of collusive capabilities yet voluntarily accept them, with adoption varying across strategic objectives and offer framings. Safeguards should therefore be tested against how a capability is described, not only against what the offer discloses: an agent that refuses an explicitly unfair tool may still accept the same tool when no one tells it that the tool is unfair.

AI Use Statement

Large Language Models (LLMs) play two distinct roles in this work. The twelve LLMs identified in Section 3 are our experimental subjects; their outputs constitute the data we report and analyze. Separately, we used LLM-based writing assistants at the manuscript stage for sentence-level proofreading, grammar checking, and stylistic polishing. LLMs were not used to design the experimental protocols, analyze the data, or interpret the results.

Ethics Statement

This work aims to improve the safety of multi-agent systems by making voluntary adoption of unfair capabilities a measurable evaluation target. All experiments involve LLM agents in simulated environments, with no human participants. We intend this work to inform the development of evaluation frameworks, safeguards, and monitoring mechanisms that can support beneficial cooperation among AI agents while preventing collusive behaviour, and to encourage the community to more explicitly study collusion as a core safety challenge in LLM-based multi-agent systems.

Reproducibility Statement

We have taken several steps to ensure the reproducibility of our results. Both experimental environments, Liar’s Bar and Cleanup, are formally described in Section 2 and Appendix C, with game rules, prompts, and secret-tool descriptions provided in Appendix P and Appendix Q. All six prompt framings (V0 baseline and V1–V5 variants) and the benign-tool control prompts are reproduced verbatim in Appendix Q.6 and Appendix G. Full inference settings (decoding parameters, API versions, structured-output parsing, and parse-failure handling) are reported in Appendix D, and our statistical-analysis protocol, including effect sizes and placebo-matched baseline controls, is documented in Appendix H. All tool-offer evaluations are replicated across 5 independent batches, and all gameplay experiments across 3 independent random seeds {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\} for both environments, using publicly available open-weight models (loaded via HuggingFace transformers) and provider APIs. Inference for 7B open-weight models was performed on a single NVIDIA H100 80 GB GPU with 16 CPU cores and 64 GB of host RAM per job. Inference for larger open-weight models used 2×2{\times}H100 80 GB with 32 CPU cores and 256 GB of host RAM. We will release the complete source code, experiment scripts, and step-by-step replication instructions upon acceptance to facilitate further extension of our framework.
